title: DAVID NEVER RETURNED TO THE TEN CONCUBINES ABSALOM HAD TAKEN—THEY LIVED LIKE WIDOWS
paragraphs: DAVID NEVER RETURNED TO THE TEN CONCUBINES ABSALOM HAD TAKEN—THEY LIVED LIKE WIDOWS

He came back to Jerusalem. He reclaimed his palace. He survived his son’s rebellion. But behind the restored doors of David’s kingdom were ten women whose lives would never return to what they had been—and one haunting Hebrew phrase exposes just how devastating the consequences of sin can become.
There is a sentence buried in 2 Samuel that is easy to read too quickly.
It comes after rebellion.
After betrayal.
After a father has been driven from Jerusalem by his own son.
After Absalom has died.
After David has wept one of the most agonizing cries recorded in Scripture:
“O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom!”
Eventually David returns to Jerusalem.
The throne is still his.
The palace is still standing.
The rebellion has failed.
The king has come home.
You might expect the story to begin settling down.
Instead, almost immediately, Scripture takes us behind the palace walls and makes us look at ten women.
Not soldiers.
Not generals.
Not politicians.
Ten women.
Women David had left behind.
Women Absalom had taken.
Women who would spend the rest of their lives in a condition Scripture describes with words so painfully strange that they should stop us in our tracks:
“living in widowhood.”
Except their husband was still alive.
The Hebrew of 2 Samuel 20:3 ends with the striking expression:
אַלְמְנוּת חַיּוּת — ’almenut ḥayyut

Literally, the language conveys the condition of living in widowhood. The Hebrew text describes them as shut away until the day of their death, and translations capture the expression as “living in widowhood,” “living as widows,” or “living as if in widowhood.”
Read that again.
Their husband had returned.
Their husband was alive.
Their husband was king.
Their material needs were provided for.
Yet they lived like widows.
And suddenly this obscure verse becomes unbearably human.
Because some consequences do not disappear when the crisis ends.
Some wounds remain after everybody else has gone home.
Some people survive another person’s sin only to discover that survival and restoration are not always the same thing.
And if you have ever wondered whether Scripture understands what it feels like to live with consequences you did not personally create, stay with these ten women for a moment.
Their story did not begin in 2 Samuel 20.

When Absalom’s rebellion forced David to flee Jerusalem, 2 Samuel 15:16 tells us that David left ten concubines behind “to keep the house”—to care for the palace. The Hebrew identifies them as עֶשֶׂר נָשִׁים פִּלַגְשִׁים — ‘eser nashim pilagshim, ten women, concubines.
David fled.
They remained.
Then Absalom entered Jerusalem.
And what happened next was not merely sexual behavior. It was a calculated political act of humiliation and royal usurpation.
Ahithophel advised Absalom to go in to his father’s concubines. A tent was then pitched on the roof, and 2 Samuel 16:22 says Absalom went in to them “in the sight of all Israel.”
Do not rush past that roof.
Because another terrible memory hangs over David’s rooftop.
Years earlier, David had walked on the roof of his palace and seen Bathsheba.
What followed was adultery, abuse of royal power, deception, the arranged death of Uriah, and an attempt to hide what had happened.
David thought the darkness could cover it.
God sent Nathan.

And Nathan told him that what David had done secretly would bring consequences into the open. In 2 Samuel 12:11–12, the judgment announced against David’s house included the shocking declaration that another would take his wives openly, “in the sight of all Israel.”
Then, chapters later, there is Absalom.
There is the roof.
There are the women.
There is all Israel watching.
The biblical narrator is forcing us to remember.
Sin travels farther than the sinner imagines.
David was forgiven when he confessed his sin. That is crucial. When David said, “I have sinned against the LORD,” Nathan answered, “The LORD also hath put away thy sin” (2 Samuel 12:13).
Grace was real.
Forgiveness was real.
But forgiveness did not magically erase every earthly consequence.
That distinction matters enormously.
Some Christians secretly believe that if repentance is genuine, every consequence should immediately disappear.
The Bible never promises that.
You can be forgiven and still have relationships to repair.
Forgiven and still have scars.
Forgiven and still need to confess what you did to another person.
Forgiven and still have children affected by choices you regret.
Forgiven and still need accountability.
Forgiven and still reap consequences from seeds you wish you had never planted.
Forgiveness means your sin no longer condemns you before God when you are in Christ.
It does not mean sin was harmless.
Look at David.
Then look at the ten women.
When David finally returned to Jerusalem, Scripture says:

“And David came to his house at Jerusalem; and the king took the ten women his concubines, whom he had left to keep the house, and put them in ward, and fed them, but went not in unto them. So they were shut up unto the day of their death, living in widowhood.”
—2 Samuel 20:3, KJV
That ending hurts.
“But went not in unto them.”
He provided for them.
But he never resumed sexual relations with them.
They remained confined until their deaths.
And here we must be careful.
Scripture does not tell us that these women seduced Absalom.
It does not tell us they invited what happened.
It does not give us access to their private thoughts, choices, fears, or degree of agency in the event.
Therefore we should not invent guilt where God’s Word does not assign it.

Some older commentators speculated about the women’s responsibility, while others understood their confinement as arising from the conventions surrounding the royal harem after Absalom had appropriated them. But the biblical text itself simply tells us what Absalom did and what David subsequently did; it does not narrate the women’s consent or motives.
That distinction matters.
Especially to the wounded.
Especially to the person who has carried shame for something someone else did to them.
Especially to someone who has confused what happened to them with what defines them.
Human beings are very good at handing shame to the wounded.
Jesus is not.
And perhaps that is where this ancient palace suddenly becomes frighteningly modern.
Because you may know what it feels like to be one of the people left behind after somebody else’s disaster.
Maybe your father’s addiction changed your childhood.
Maybe your spouse’s betrayal changed how easily you trust.
Maybe someone abused power over you and walked away while you carried the memories.
Maybe somebody made one selfish decision that altered your family for twenty years.
Maybe you are living inside consequences you never voted for.
Maybe everybody remembers the name of the person who caused the scandal…
but almost nobody remembers yours.
People remember David.
People remember Absalom.
People remember Bathsheba.
People remember Nathan.
People remember Ahithophel.
But ask most believers to name the ten women of 2 Samuel 20:3.
They cannot.
Scripture does not even give us their names here.
Yet God saw them.
That may be the sentence someone reading this desperately needed.
God saw them.
The biblical narrative did not allow them to disappear completely.
One verse preserved their tragedy for thousands of years.
Kings fought.
Armies marched.
Rebellions rose and collapsed.
Men competed for thrones.
And the Holy Spirit inspired Scripture that stopped long enough to tell us that ten women spent the remainder of their lives living like widows.
Heaven notices people history overlooks.
And maybe heaven has noticed you too.
But there is another truth here that we cannot soften.
David's household did not become this fractured overnight.
Long before Absalom’s rebellion, God had already given Israel’s kings a warning. Deuteronomy 17:17 commanded that the king was not to multiply wives for himself.
David was a man after God’s own heart, but “man after God’s own heart” never meant “man without grievous sin.”
The Bible refuses to airbrush its heroes.
That is one reason Scripture is so devastatingly believable.
David can kill Goliath in faith…
and later abuse his royal power terribly.
He can write psalms that have comforted broken hearts for three thousand years…
and still leave devastation inside his own family.
He can worship passionately…
and fail catastrophically.
He can genuinely repent…
and still live long enough to watch consequences unfold.
The Bible does not need David to be spotless.
Because David is not the Savior.
Jesus is.
And that changes everything.
If you read the Old Testament searching for flawless human heroes, eventually every human throne disappoints you.
David points beyond himself.
We need a better King.
A King who does not exploit the vulnerable.
A King who does not take what belongs to another.
A King whose private life does not contradict His public righteousness.
A King who does not abandon His people when rebellion comes.
A King who does not merely provide bread from a distance but comes personally to the broken.
A King who touches lepers.
Receives outcasts.
Defends the condemned.
Calls sinners to repentance.
Forgives the guilty.
Restores the ruined.
And willingly gives Himself for people who rebelled against Him.
Jesus Christ is that King.
David returned to Jerusalem and entered his palace.
Jesus entered Jerusalem knowing He was going to a cross.
David's kingdom was shaken by his son's rebellion.
Jesus came into a world already in rebellion against God.
David survived while Absalom died.
Jesus, the sinless Son, willingly died so rebels could live.
Do you see the reversal?
At Calvary, the innocent King bears the judgment of the guilty.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
This is where scandal collides with grace.
Not cheap grace.
Not grace that calls evil good.
Not grace that pretends consequences do not matter.
Grace with nail wounds.
Grace that tells the truth about sin because sin was serious enough to require the cross.
Grace that looks at repentant sinners and says their worst chapter does not have authority to write their final chapter.
David sinned.
David was exposed.
David repented.
David was forgiven.
David suffered consequences.
And still…
God's redemptive plan continued.
Eventually, through David's royal line, according to the flesh, came Jesus Christ.
Think about that.
God did not call David's evil good.
God did not erase the seriousness of his sin.
God did not pretend innocent people had not been affected.
Yet human failure could not derail God's redemptive purpose.
That is the difference between covering scandal and redeeming sinners.
The Gospel does not say:
“It never happened.”
The Gospel says:
“It will not have the final word.”
Maybe that is why you found this article.
Perhaps there is a chapter you keep trying to tear out of your story.
Something you did.
Something done to you.
A marriage that collapsed.
A secret nobody knows.
An addiction you keep feeding while telling everyone you are fine.
A betrayal you cannot undo.
A childhood wound that still follows you into adult rooms.
A private compromise beneath a public Christian image.
You know how to smile at church.
You know when to say “Amen.”
You know which verse to post.
But when everything becomes quiet, you still hear the chains moving inside rooms nobody else can see.
Listen carefully.
Jesus did not come to improve your disguise.
He came to save you.
There is an enormous difference.
Repentance is not learning how to hide the evidence more successfully.
Repentance is bringing the truth into God's light.
David learned painfully that hidden sin does not remain safely hidden.
You can bury something from people.
You cannot bury it from God.
Yet the terrifying holiness of God is not the end of the Gospel story.
The God who sees everything is also the God who sent His Son.
That means you do not need to clean yourself before coming to Christ.
You come because you cannot cleanse yourself.
You confess.
You repent.
You stop defending what God calls sin.
You stop calling chains “freedom.”
You stop calling compromise “complicated.”
You stop negotiating with the thing crucifying your soul.
And you run to Jesus.
Not because your sin is small.
Because His grace is greater.
Not because consequences are imaginary.
Because condemnation does not belong to those who are in Christ Jesus.
Not because your past suddenly becomes beautiful.
Because Christ can take a story scarred by sin and make even the scars testify that mercy came.
That is From Scandal to Grace.
Not scandal to denial.
Not scandal to religious reputation management.
Not scandal to pretending.
Scandal…
to confession.
Confession…
to repentance.
Repentance…
to mercy.
Mercy…
to restoration.
And restoration…
to a life that begins telling other broken people:
There is still a Savior.
Maybe you identify with David today.
Then repent.
Stop hiding.
There is mercy in Christ.
Maybe you identify more with those ten unnamed women.
Then hear this carefully:
What someone did to you is not the measure of your worth before God.
You are not merely somebody's aftermath.
You are not merely somebody's scandal.

And although this passage does not give us the rest of those women's inner stories, the whole counsel of Scripture reveals a God who repeatedly sees the afflicted, hears the brokenhearted, and draws near to those who cry to Him.
Maybe you are Absalom in this story—angry, ambitious, wounded, and using your pain as permission to wound others.
Stop before another person becomes collateral damage in your rebellion.
Pain does not become righteousness simply because it has a reason.
Bring it to Christ.
Maybe you are standing on a rooftop spiritually right now, one decision away from creating consequences you cannot predict.
Walk away.
Close the conversation.
Delete the secret account.
Confess the affair.
Tell someone about the addiction.
Return what is not yours.
Ask forgiveness.
Get accountable.
Run from temptation.
Do not wait until tomorrow's consequences explain today's warning.
Sin always promises control.
Then sends invoices.
Jesus offers something radically different.
Surrender.
Forgiveness.
A new heart.
A new Master.
A new direction.
Life.
Be honest.
Someone reading your words may realize they are not the only person still fighting.
And if somebody came to your mind while reading this, do not simply think about them.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to preach down at them.

Sharing biblical truth is not a substitute for obedience, prayer, generosity, local-church faithfulness, or personally proclaiming Christ. But it can be one simple act of placing the Gospel where another wounded person may encounter it.
Because one day you may need to remember:
forgiveness does not mean sin was harmless, consequences do not mean grace has failed, and scars do not mean Jesus has finished writing.

And if Gospel Warrior has been feeding your faith, challenging your compromises, strengthening your walk with Christ, or helping you place biblical truth in front of people who desperately need it, consider staying close and supporting this ministry.
More importantly, the purpose is deeper discipleship.
Biblical nourishment.
Conviction.
Encouragement.
Accountability.
Spiritual sharpening.
A community continually being pointed away from itself and back to Jesus Christ.
But before you leave this story, go back one last time.
Back through the palace doors.
Back past David.
Back past Absalom.
Back past the throne.
Back to ten unnamed women living out their days in a condition Scripture calls widowhood.
We do not know their private thoughts.
We do not know the conversations they had behind those guarded doors.
We do not know whether they cried at night.
We do not know whether they ever imagined their story would still be read thousands of years later.
So we will not invent what God chose not to reveal.
But we know this:
Their pain became part of a biblical warning that still speaks.
Sin reaches farther than we think.
Power can wound people who never asked to become part of the scandal.
Forgiveness is real.
Consequences are real.
Grace is real.
And David, for all his greatness, was never enough.
We needed another King.
We needed Jesus.
The King who entered our scandal without participating in our sin.
The King who carried our shame without deserving it.
The King who received wounds so wounded sinners could be reconciled to God.
The King who walked into death and walked back out.
So whatever room you believe your past has locked you inside…
do not mistake the room for the ending.
Bring your guilt to Christ.
Bring your wounds to Christ.
Bring your anger.
Your secrets.
Your regrets.
Your shame.
Your shattered family.
Your consequences.
Your unanswered questions.
Bring the pieces.
Because the Gospel has never been about pretending the pieces were never broken.
It is about what happens when the broken pieces finally reach the hands of the Redeemer.
Your scandal may explain some of your scars—but only Jesus gets to write the final sentence.
